frequency_question: How often do structural institutional frictions (such as sub-national vetoes or constitutional requirements for state-level concurrence) successfully block the renewal of an expiring transboundary water treaty within the designated renewal window?
membership_rule: Includes any bilateral or multi-lateral transboundary water treaty involving a federal republic where lower-tier governments possess constitutional or practical veto power over water allocation, undergoing mandatory renewal or extension processes.

cases.name: Indus Waters Treaty implementation adjustments and friction points
Mahakali Treaty (India-Nepal) ratification and supplementary protocols
Farakka Barrage initial sharing arrangement extensions
Teesta River interim water sharing agreement stalling due to West Bengal state opposition
Colorado River Basin delivery and shortage guidelines renegotiation (US-Mexico)
Lesotho Highlands Water Project Phase II operational protocol renewals

coverage_note: 6 named cases representing major federal-state riparian negotiations globally within the designated timeframe.
known_gaps: Excludes minor administrative water committee renewals that do not reach the treaty-signing executive level.
skeleton: Total relevant transboundary water treaty renewal attempts involving federal-state friction points divided by those successfully blocked by structural friction.
multiplier: 1 obstruction resulting in failure out of 6 major federal-state riparian friction instances over 30 years.
validity_reason: Institutional frameworks governing federal-state water rights and transboundary negotiations evolve slowly over decades.
